title: FLEX: Unifying Evaluation for Few-Shot NLP
body_text:
FLEET: Unifying Evaluation for Few-Shot NLP



Anonymous

 Author(s)

AfﬁliationAddress email



Abstract Few-shot NLP research is highly active, yet conducted in disjoint research threads 1 with evaluation suites that lack challenging-yet-realistic testing setups and fail to 2 employ careful experimental design. Consequently, the community does not know 3 which techniques perform best or even if they outperform simple baselines. We 4 formulate desiderata for an ideal few-shot NLP benchmark and present FLEET, 1 5 the ﬁrst benchmark, public leaderboard, and framework that provides uniﬁed, 6 comprehensive measurement for few-shot NLP techniques. FLEET incorporates 7 and introduces new best practices for few-shot evaluation, including measurement 8 of four transfer settings, textual labels for zero-shot evaluation, and a principled 9 approach to benchmark design that optimizes statistical accuracy while keeping 10 evaluation costs accessible to researchers without large compute resources. We 11 also present UniFew, a simple yet strong baseline model with uniﬁed pretraining 12 and ﬁnetuning prompt format. UniFew achieves results competitive with popular 13 meta-learning procedures and recent prompt-based approaches, while eschewing 14 their complex machinery. 15



1 Introduction 16

 Few-shot learning, the challenge of learning from a small number of examples, is critical for 17 developing efﬁcient, robust NLP techniques [65, 72]. In recent years, separate threads of few-shot 18 NLP research have pursued goals like generalization to new classes [e

.

 g., 4, 24], adaptation to new 19 domains and tasks [e.g., 2, 3, 20]

,

 and direct application of pretrained language models (LMs) [e

.

 g., 20 9, 23, 50, 51]. Unfortunately, despite the shared goal of advancing few-shot NLP techniques, the 21 community does not know which techniques work best or even if they perform better than simple 22 baselines. Evaluation suites across these research threads are disjoint, lack challenging-yet-realistic 23 testing setups (e.g., class imbalance, variable training set sizes, etc.)

,

 and do not employ careful 24 experimental design to ensure accurate and precise evaluation estimates and minimal computational 25 burden. Prior work in few-shot learning outside of NLP serves as a stark warning of the consequences 26 of improper measurement: Dhillon et al. [18] showed that techniques from several years of prior 27 work did not make clear progress due to large overlapping accuracy distributions and, moreover, do 28 not outperform a simple, carefully-tuned baseline. 29 As such, a high-quality benchmark is urgently needed to enable rigorous comparison of techniques 30 across disjoint, highly-active threads of few-shot NLP research. But what should such an evaluation 31 suite look like? Some best practices for evaluation of few-shot methods have been introduced in the 32 computer vision (CV) literature [18, 61] and should be applied to NLP. However, unifying few-shot 33 NLP work introduces new challenges. For example, the benchmark needs to test all types of transfer 34 studied in separate research threads to measure progress on new techniques that make gains in each 35 of these important generalization settings (§2). Also, given the importance of zero-shot learning 36 1 https://github.com/anonymous . Submitted to 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2021). Do not distribute. 160 16 37 7 18 8 20 and learning from task descriptions [28, 67], the benchmark needs to include zero-shot episodes 37 and textual labels to enable measuring progress for models that do not use conventional supervised 38 training, including methods that leverage the latent knowledge in pretrained LMs [9, 23, 74]. Further, 39 the benchmark must accommodate new, computationally-expensive approaches, without overly 40 reducing the number of evaluation episodes at the expense of statistical accuracy [2, 23, 71]. 41 In this paper, we tackle these issues by contributing the following: 42 • Desiderata (§3) for few-shot NLP benchmarks, which include best practices from CV and introduce 43 new ones that enable uniﬁed, comprehensive, low-cost measurement across several disjoint few- 44 shot NLP research threads. 45 • FLEET (§4)— F ew-shot L anguag E E valua T ion— a uniﬁed benchmark that meets these desiderata. 46 Our benchmark includes the ﬁrst evaluation protocol that efﬁciently tests across four few-shot 47 transfer settings, 2 and includes a public leaderboard for few-shot NLP that covers 20 datasets 48 across diverse NLP tasks (e.g., NLI, relation classiﬁcation , entity typing). Table 1 summarizes key 49 differences between FLEET and other few -shot NLP evaluation suites . 50 • Novel approach to few-shot sample size design (§5) that optimizes for the benchmark’s statis- 51 tical accuracy and precision while keeping computational costs accessible to a broad range of 52 researchers. Our analysis reveals the pitfalls of few-episode designs used in prior works , and 53 demonstrates a principled solution for determining the right balance of episodes to test examples. 54 • UniFew (§6), a simple but powerful baseline that formats tasks as multiple-choice questions. It 55 achieves results competitive with recent few-shot methods without extensive prompt-engineering 56 or complicated modeling or training techniques. 57 • An extensible, open-source framework for few-shot NLP model development and benchmark 58 creation, used to train UniFew and produce FLEET. Unlike existing few-shot frameworks, it 59 enables easily adding a wide range of NLP datasets and advanced sampling options. 60

2 Background and Related Work 61

 We ﬁrst provide background and notation for few-shot learning and evaluation, then discuss related 62 work in NLP and outside NLP that motivated us to create FLEET. 63 2 Few-Shot Background and Notation Broadly, modern approaches to few-shot learning are evalu- 64 ated in a three-phase procedure [62]. In the ﬁrst phase, a general-purpose pretrained model is obtained. 65 In the subsequent “meta-training” phase, 6 techniques aim to adapt the model to be well-suited for 66 few-shot generalization. Finally, a “meta-testing” phase evaluates the adapted model in new few-shot 67 prediction settings. 68 Let D be a dataset of ( x, y ) examples with full label set Y D . From it, we construct three sets of 69 episodes, corresponding to meta-training, meta-validation, and meta-testing and denoted by E train , 70 E val , and E test , respectively. Each episode in each of these sets is a few-shot problem with its own test 71 set and other attributes. Formally, each episode E is a tuple ( D E train , D E val , D E test , Y E D ) , where Y E D is a 72 sampled subset of labels in Y D and D E train | val | test are disjoint sets of examples from D with labels in 73 Y E D . 7 For each episode, the model’s objective is to correctly predict labels for examples D E test . To 74 accomplish this, models make use of labeled examples in D E train , which is typically conﬁgured such 75 that each label i in Y E D has K Ei provided examples; K Ei is known as the shot , and the setting when a 76 class has no examples in D E train (i.e., K Ei = 0 ) is called zero-shot . 77 Few-Shot Evaluation in NLP Research in few-shot NLP has proceeded in several parallel threads, 78 each focused on a different type of transfer ability [72]. Each thread has separate evaluation practices, 79 and the vast majority of few-shot NLP research has limited to single type of transfer (see Table 1). 80 Here, we describe these types of transfer and their evaluation practices. 81 Following CV literature [61, 62], one thread of few-shot NLP focuses on class transfer , the problem 82 of generalizing from a supervised set of classes at meta-train time to a different set of classes from 83 the same dataset at meta-test time. Evaluation typically requires splitting classes Y D into Y D train , 84 Y D val and Y D test disjoint subsets. Class transfer has been studied on many text classiﬁcation tasks [4], 85 including relation classiﬁcation [24, 27, 58], intent classiﬁcation [34, 58], inter alia. In contrast, 86 domain transfer keeps the same classes between meta-training and meta-testing but changes the 87 textual domain (e.g., generalizing from MNLI to science-focused SciTail [3, 20]). Evaluation then 88 requires identifying pairs of datasets with the same classes Y D where one’s episodes are assigned to 89 E train and the other’s to E test . Domain transfer has also been studied on many tasks [2, 3], including 90 dialogue intent detection & slot tagging [30], sentiment classiﬁcation [73], NLI [20], machine 91 translation [26, 53]. 92 Researchers have also begun to study task transfer , the problem of generalizing from a set of 93 tasks at meta-train time to unseen tasks at meta-test time. Evaluation requires tasks (e.g., NLI) 94 appearing in E test to not appear in E train or E val . Prior work has used GLUE tasks [64] for meta-training 95 before meta-testing on tasks such as entity typing [2, 3], while other work instead used GLUE for 96 meta-testing [20]. Very recent work has studied task transfer over a large set of datasets [71]. A 97 limited amount of work evaluates both domain and task transfer [2, 3, 20]. An important emerging 98 line of work not noted by Yin [72] is pretraining transfer , the problem of whether pretrained 99 language models can perform well at meta-test time without any meta-training. Evaluation in this 100 setting requires E train , E val = ∅ . Prior work has shown that pretrained language models are capable 101 of surprising performance on many few-shot tasks, even without ﬁne-tuning [9]. More recent work, 102 mainly focusing on text classiﬁcation, has reported further gains with cloze-style formats [50, 51, 59], 103 prompt engineering [23], or calibration [74]. FLEET is designed to exercise all four of these transfer 104 types from previous work. 105 Few-Shot Evaluation Outside NLP The few-shot learning literature has largely focused on image 106 classiﬁcation, with the introduction of increasingly complex meta-learning algorithms [e.g., 22, 107 36, 49, 55, 62]. However, more recent work has shown that simple ﬁne-tuning baselines are in fact 108 competitive, and attribute this delayed discovery to problematic evaluation methodology [14, 18]. 109 FLEET adopts recommended methodology [18, 61], and we introduce an analogous baseline to 110 provide a strong measurement foundation for few-shot NLP. 111 6 Meta-training may include a “meta-validation" component, for validating generalization. 7 In the few-shot literature, D E train and D E test are also called the support and query sets, and |Y E D | the way . 3

3 Desiderata for Few-Shot NLP Evaluation

 112 We now enumerate key desiderata for a few-shot NLP benchmark capable of solving the urgent 113 problems with few-shot NLP evaluation, including separate evaluations for each transfer type (§2) 114 and failure to incorporate best measurement practices from other domains (§2). 115 Diversity of transfer types To make NLP models broadly useful, few-shot NLP techniques must be 116 capable of class, domain, and task transfer. Moreover, techniques should make use of the relevant 117 supervision provided during meta-training to increase performance compared to the pretraining 118 transfer setting. The benchmark should measure all four transfer settings to ensure that the community 119 develops techniques that improve on strong pretraining transfer baselines, and enable comparison 120 across these currently separate threads of research. 121 Variable number of shots and classes To better simulate a variety of real-world scenarios, the 122 benchmark should include a variety of training set sizes and number of classes [61]. Testing 123 robustness to these factors is crucial; few-shot techniques are often sensitive to changes in these 124 factors [11], yet all prior few-shot NLP evaluations we are aware of used a ﬁxed number of training 125 shots and classes, known in advance during meta-training. 126 Unbalanced training sets The benchmark should also include unbalanced training sets with different 127 training shots per class, another realistic setting adopted by CV benchmarks [61]. Class imbalance 128 has also been observed to degrade performance [10, 41], yet prior few-shot NLP evaluations do not 129 include this setting either. 130 Textual labels While numerical label values are often used in classiﬁcation tasks, descriptive textual 131 labels are also present for many tasks. Making these textual labels available for use by few-shot 132 techniques enables the development of techniques that can leverage the class name, like in-context 133 learning [9] and template generation [23]. Textual labels are crucial in particular for zero-shot 134 evaluation. 135 Zero-shot evaluation We believe zero-shot evaluation is integral to the goals of few-shot evaluation. 136 Similar to the motivation for measuring pretraining transfer, zero-shot evaluation is an important use 137 case and also provides a strong baseline for some tasks. In the absence of training examples, textual 138 class labels or richer task descriptions [68] must be provided. Some recent NLP work [e.g., 9, 23] 139 evaluated with zero training shots, but most [e.g., 2, 4, 71] did not. 140 No extra meta-testing data We believe the benchmark should not provide validation data ( D E val = 141 ∅ , ∀ E ∈ E test ) or unlabeled data for meta-testing tasks, since few-shot learning seeks to enable high 142 performance in environments where collecting additional data is costly. 8 Variation in these dimensions 143 in prior NLP work makes comparison of results extremely difﬁcult because it is often under-reported 144 and gives unfair advantage to approaches that leverage such data [45]. For example, per-episode 145 hyperparameter tuning on extra data has been shown to greatly inﬂate evaluation scores [23]. Bao 146 et al. [4], Tam et al. [59] follow our suggested approach, but other researchers have used many other 147 settings, from validation sets of various sizes [9, 23] to no validation set but a large set of unlabeled 148 examples [50, 51]. 149 Principled sample size design Promising few-shot techniques can incur signiﬁcant computational 150 cost per episode, e.g., due to ﬁne-tuning model parameters [3], searching for prompts [23], inter 151 alia. To alleviate these costs, related works often evaluate with a limited number of episodes, which 152 precludes statistically accurate or precise performance estimates. We believe the benchmark’s test 153 sample size should be optimized to enable proper performance evaluation for such techniques, while 154 ensuring the computational burden is inclusive toward researchers without large compute resources. 155 Proper reporting of CIs, SDs, and individual results The benchmark should report conﬁdence 156 intervals (CIs) of performance estimates and follow recent guidelines [18] to report standard deviations 157 (SDs) for understanding variability. Moreover, we newly advocate for controlling for the same 158 sampled few-shot episodes across all methods and reporting individual episode results, so that 159 researchers can run higher-powered paired statistical tests when comparing results [21], crucial when 160 the benchmark has been optimized for low evaluation budgets. 161 8 Unlabeled data collection can be costly too, e.g. due to manual ﬁltering [15]. 4

4 The FLEET Benchmark

 162 FLEET is a unifying, rigorous benchmark for few-shot learning in NLP, which implements the 163 desiderata outlined in the previous section. In this section, we describe detailed design decisions and 164 our few-shot NLP framework (§4.4), which we are releasing to facilitate easily adding NLP datasets 165 and advanced sampling options to future benchmarks. 166

4.1 Task and Dataset Selection

 167 Following GLUE [64] and other prior work [2, 4, 23, 74], we focus on tasks formatted as classiﬁca- 168 tion. Despite recent advances, NLP state-of-the-art models remain signiﬁcantly worse than human 169 performance on many text classiﬁcation tasks, particularly in the few-shot setting. Automatic scoring 170 of classiﬁcation tasks is also more reliable than text generation tasks. 171 We selected datasets across three recent few-shot NLP evaluation suites, which separately studied 172 class transfer [4], domain and task transfer [2, 3], and pretraining transfer [23]. FLEET includes a 173 broad mix of tasks (NLI, question classiﬁcation, entity typing, relation classiﬁcation, and sentiment 174 analysis) and formats (document, sentence, sentence pair). More complete dataset and license details 175 are available in subsequent subsections and Appendix A. 176

4.2 Meta-Evaluation Protocols

 177 As discussed earlier, FLEET evaluates four different types of transfer: Class, Domain, Task and 178 Pretraining Transfer. To support all types, we report results to the FLEET benchmark both without 179 meta-training (pretraining-only) and with meta-training. This reporting scheme evaluates the perfor- 180 mance of the basic pretrained model and the beneﬁt (or lack thereof) of meta-training. A similar 181 reporting scheme was proposed by Triantaﬁllou et al. [61]. 182 Pretraining-Only In this setting, the pretrained model is directly meta-tested on FLEET without any 183 additional training. This is the Pretraining Transfer setting, and it is the most difﬁcult, but given the 184 recent success of pretrained models in NLP for few-shot learning [9, 23], we believe that comparison 185 to models without any meta-training is important for NLP tasks. 186 Meta-Trained In this setting, the model is meta-trained then meta-tested on FLEET. We carefully 187 selected and split datasets across meta-train/validation/test in order to enable testing of Class, Domain, 188 and Task transfer with a single meta-training phase (to reduce computational burden). Datasets 189 involved in each transfer setting (detailed split information in Table 4 in Appendix A): 190 • Class Transfer : FewRel [27], HuffPost [40], Amazon [29], 20News [35], and Reuters [38] take 191 part in meta-training and meta-testing but with different classes. 192 • Domain Transfer : MR [44], CR [31], SNLI [8], and SciTail [33] are only in the meta-testing phase, 193 but the corresponding sentiment and NLI datasets exist in the meta-training phase (MNLI [69], 194 QNLI [47], and SST-2 [56]). 195 • Task Transfer : Subj [43], TREC [63], and CoNLL [60] are also for meta-testing only, and they 196 represent tasks that the model does not encounter during meta-training. 197 Instead of per-episode hyperparameter tuning, we provide meta-validation episodes E val for learning 198 (during meta-training) global hyperparameters that work across all episodes. Speciﬁcally, the meta- 199 validation dataset splits (see Table 4) consist of CoLa [66] for task transfer, WNLI [37] for domain 200 transfer, and the validation splits used by Bao et al. [4] for all class transfer datasets. Following [2], 201 we also include meta-training datasets MRPC [19], RTE [5, 7, 16, 25], and QQP [64]. 202

4.3 Episode Sampling

 203 We describe how FLEET samples meta-testing episodes E test . For meta-training, we allow users to 204 sample from E train , E val in any way, or directly use the underlying dataset splits. 205 Number of classes For Class Transfer datasets, FLEET aims to evaluate model robustness to a 206 variable number of classes. When constructing episode E from one of these datasets D , FLEET 207 samples an episode-speciﬁc number of classes from dataset D , the sampler picks a random number 208 5 Number of shots Following prior work outside NLP [42, 61], FLEET samples the training shot 211 independently for each episode E and class i , as K Ei ∼ Unif( K min , K max ) , where K min = 1 . 212 Given strong performance of NLP models with few or even zero examples [9, 68] and following 213 prior work [4], we set the limit K max = 5 . Separately, we allocate an equal number of episodes as 214 zero-shot, where we instead set D E train = ∅ (equivalently, K Ei = 0 , ∀ i ). 215

4.4 Extensible Framework for Benchmark Creation and Model Training & Evaluation

 216 Alongside the FLEET benchmark, we release an extensible, highly-conﬁgurable Python framework, 217 which we used to generate FLEET (and earlier benchmarks), and train and evaluate our models. 218 Unlike existing meta-learning frameworks (e.g., Torchmeta [17], learn2learn [1]), our framework 219 makes available a wide range of community-contributed NLP datasets and utilities via HuggingFace 220 Datasets [70] 10 . Our code also provides advanced sampling utilities (e.g., for class imbalance), 221 ensures reproducibility by checksumming generated episodes, and reports all recommended statistics. 222

5 Sample Size: Balancing Statistical Measurement and Computational Cost 223

 We demonstrate a principled approach to determining the optimal sample size conﬁguration in our 224 few-shot benchmark. A proper benchmark should produce performance estimates that are accurate , 225 close to the true value, and precise , low variance. A large (test) sample size can achieve this, yet must 226 be considered alongside computational cost so that a broad community of researchers with differing 227 amounts of compute resources can participate. This decision is further complicated in the few-shot 228 setting, where sample size refers to both the number of test episodes |E test | and the number of test 229 examples |D E test | per episode E ∈ E test . For practicality, we consider |D test | , the mean |D E test | across all 230 episodes, rather than every |D E test | . It remains unknown how one should best distribute test examples 231 between |E test | and |D test | : More episodes each with fewer examples, or fewer episodes each with 232 many examples? Prior work has been inconsistent in this regard. For example, Gao et al. [23] used 233 |E test | = 5 and large |D test | , while Bao et al. [4] used |E test | = 1000 and much smaller |D test | . 234 Inspired by simulation techniques for informing statistically-powered experimental design [12], we 235 study how different conﬁgurations of |E test | and |D test | across different compute budgets C impact the 236 9 We limit to 10 classes to avoid undue burden on in-context approaches that ﬁt examples in memory [9], and use a lower bound of 5 classes to match prior work [4]. 10 Apache License 2.0. Full license details for all software dependencies available in Appendix H. 6 accuracy and precision of our estimated CIs, speciﬁcally with respect to coverage probability [48] 237 and width . First, we estimate per-episode and per-test-example costs of our few-shot baseline (§6) 238 to obtain valid ( C, |E test | , |D test | ) conﬁgurations s.t. the full benchmark completes within given C 239 (GPU-hours). 11 Then, for each ( C, |E test | , |D test | ) , we perform 1000 simulation runs, in which each 240 run samples predictions under a true model accuracy µ acc and computes a single 95% CI, its width, 241 and whether it correctly covers µ acc . Averaging over simulation runs gives us estimates for the 242 coverage probability and width of our benchmark’s CI for a single ( C, |E test | , |D test | ) . We repeat this 243 whole procedure for different µ acc ∈ { 0 . 3 , 0 . 35 , . . . , 0 . 95 } to cover a wide range of possible model 244 performances observed across many datasets (see Table 3). 245 Figure 1 shows CI coverage probability and width for many ( C, |E test | , |D test | ) conﬁgurations. First, 246 we ﬁnd in Figure 1a that sufﬁciently-many test episodes (i.e. |E test | > 60 ) is needed to guarantee 247 coverage probability of our CIs is within one percentage point of the target 95%, a trend that holds 248 regardless of compute budget. Small |E test | also corresponds to large CI widths across all considered 249 budgets in Figure 1b. This suggests that the choices of |E test | = 1 , 5 , 10 in prior work [3, 23, 51, 71] 250 can mean inaccurate and wide CIs, while choices of |E test | = 1000 [4] can be prohibitively costly for 251 methods with high training cost. 252 Next, Figure 1b reveals (i) diminishing returns in CI width (decrease in y -axis) as compute increases, 253 and (ii) existence of an optimal balance between |E test | and |D test | for each budget. Restricting 254 our consideration to budgets with optima satisfying |E test | > 60 , the minimum viable budget is 36 255 GPU-hours. Then, assessing the marginal beneﬁt of each 12 GPU-hour budget increase in terms of 256 marginal reduction in CI width between optima, we arrive at our FLEET conﬁguration of |E test | = 90 257 and |D test | ≈ 470 under a budget of C = 48 GPU-hours. 12 Further details are in Appendix B. 258

6 UniFew: A Simple yet Powerful Baseline 259

 Despite their encouraging results, existing works on few-shot learning are based on either customized 260 and often complex meta-learning algorithms [2, 3, 4, 54], heavy engineering of textual descriptions 261 or prompts [23, 50, 74], ordering of training examples [39, 51], extensive hyperparameter tuning 262 on held-out sets [23, 39, 50], or custom learning algorithms [50, 59]. We present UniFew, a strong 263 baseline across all transfer settings and datasets tested, that eschews the need for incorporating the 264 above-mentioned complexities and challenges. 265 UniFew is a prompt-based model [51], a class of models that tailor the input/output format of their 266 data to match the format used during pretraining. While this technique allows them to perform a task 267 without the need for additional classiﬁcation layers, prompt-based models are typically sensitive to the 268 choice of the prompts, which can require extensive search, trial-and-error, and even additional models 269 to get right [23, 74]. To avoid this issue while still leveraging the strong capabilities of pretrained 270 models, UniFew (1) converts examples into multiple-choice question-answer (QA) format, and (2) 271 uses UniﬁedQA [32], a T5 [46] model further pretrained on a large collection of QA pairs. 13,14 272 Compared to other prompt-based models, UniFew has two main strengths. First, the prompt design 273 problem is much simpler because UniﬁedQA questions had well-deﬁned formats. For example, we 274 need only two prompt templates to cover 19 of the 20 datasets in FLEET, while prior works have 275 needed specialized prompts for each dataset. Second, UniﬁedQA’s multiple-choice format ensures 276 the model outputs a valid class label, without the need for learned or manually-deﬁned mappings 277 required for other prompt-based methods [23, 50] . 15 278 11 Costs estimated using a Quadro RTX-8000 GPU with 48Gb memory. For few-shot settings, model was trained with 300 steps. Per-episode and per-test-example costs were approx. 95–98 and 0.7–0.11 GPU-sec, respectively. Using a model with high per-episode cost for this analysis allows us to deﬁne a lower-bound sample size requirement; we can always test inexpensive or zero-shot models on more |E test | or D test within budget. 12 Consider budget increases 36 → 48 , 48 → 60 , 60 → 72 and 72 → 80 . The ﬁrst reduces CI width by 13%. Further increases reduce CI width by an additional 9%, 7%, and 5%, respectively. We choose C = 48 based on these diminishing returns. 13 UniﬁedQA and T5 both use Apache License 2.0. We use publicly-released large-size model weights. 14 None of the supervised datasets in the pretraining of UniﬁedQA or T5 are in FLEET. 15 In rare cases, especially for zero-shot, UniﬁedQA may generate an invalid answer (e.g., “Yes, Yes, No” instead of “Yes”). We use simple heuristics to normalize the answer in such cases. 7 We experiment with UniFew both without and with meta-training on FLEET’s meta-training data. 279 We call the meta-trained variant UniFew meta . Details about prompts and training are in Appendix C 280 and D, respectively. 281

7 Experiments

 282 Comparing UniFew with Prior Work To demonstrate the efﬁcacy of UniFew, we evaluate it 283 against state-of-the-art approaches for few-shot and meta-learning in NLP: LM-BFF [23], a language 284 model prompt-based ﬁne-tuning method, and Distributional Signatures (DS) [4] and H-SMLMT [3], 285 two state-of-the-art meta-learning techniques. Refer to Appendix E for details on these methods. 286 We compare to these methods using the datasets in FLEET to establish the quality of our baseline 287 on our benchmark. Since we constructed FLEET from disjoint subsets of datasets evaluated in each 288 of these prior works (§4.1), we compare each method with its corresponding subset of datasets. 289 Each of these prior works evaluates their methods using different experimental setups (classes, 290 number of episodes, shots) than FLEET and was not designed to handle FLEET’s challenging episode 291 characteristics like class imbalance. To enable fair comparison, we test UniFew on the exact data splits 292 released by the authors when available (H-SMLMT and LM-BFF). For DS, we sample (balanced) 293 episodes using our framework after matching their test settings (number of shots and classes, class 294 splits, etc.) and reproduce their reported results to within 1% absolute difference using their model 295 code; we use these episodes for our experiments. The results in Table 2 show that UniFew meta 296 16 Gao et al. [23]’s automatic prompt search and in-context learning are not available in the zero-shot setting, so they instead use manually-designed prompts. 17 Zero-shot results from Gao et al. [23] are on the entire test set, so there is no reported standard deviation. 18 16/16 denotes 16 shots for training plus 16 more for validation which we only use for early stopping while Gao et al. [23] use for grid-search hyperparameter tuning. 8 outperforms both H-SMLMT and DS meta-learning approaches by relatively large margins, while 297 achieving competitive results compared with LM-BFF. Note that UniFew’s strong results are without 298 meta-learning approaches, extensive prompt-engineering, or per-episode hyperparameter search. 299 Evaluating UniFew on FLEET Having established UniFew as a strong model comparable to 300 recent, state-of-the art techniques, we present its baseline results on the ﬁnal version of FLEET (with 301 class imbalance, etc.). From Table 3, we observe three ﬁndings. First, pretraining is an effective 302 technique for infusing an NLP model with the ability to perform few-shot generalization even without 303 any meta-training, as UniFew is able to score ∆ few = +16 . 2 higher when provided few examples. 304 Second, by comparing UniFew meta and UniFew, we see that meta-training has a substantial impact on 305 zero-shot performance ( ∆ meta = +23 . 9 ), but its beneﬁt, while still signiﬁcant, is less in the few-shot 306 setting ( ∆ meta = +14 . 6 ). Third, while meta-training adds roughly the same beneﬁt to zero and 307 few-shot performance for both domain and task transfer settings, meta-training disproportionately 308 beneﬁts zero-shot class transfer ( ∆ meta = +30 . 7 ) over few-shot class transfer ( ∆ meta = +8 . 5 ). Such 309 observations are made possible through uniﬁed evaluation and comparison across different transfer 310 types. The full FLEET results broken down by individual datasets are in Appendix G. 311

8 Limitations and Future Work

 312 Ultimately, we believe that a few-shot NLP benchmark should measure the abilities of language 313 models on a variety of task formats. While FLEET is currently limited in its focus solely on 314 classiﬁcation, we aim to use our new framework (§4.4) to incorporate additional task formats like 315 span selection or text generation. 316 In addition, our sample size analysis (§5) currently uses simulations that are not based on a represen- 317 tative sample of many techniques, instead focusing on our own available training estimates. We plan 318 to gather compute estimates from community submissions to FLEET to reﬁne our conﬁgurations. 319 Our public leaderboard currently provides limited support for detailed comparisons between sub- 320 missions based on properties of techniques. For example, approaches may vary in terms of model 321 characteristics (e.g., number of parameters), data and supervision used during pretraining, amount of 322 compute, etc. We encourage users of FLEET to report all these factors to enable the community to 323 analyze and make progress on important sub-spaces in the overall few-shot technique design space. 324 Finally, we believe the beneﬁts of improving few-shot NLP techniques outweigh potential risks, but 325 we acknowledge potential harms associated with language models [6, 13, 52, 57]. We provide more 326 discussion in Appendix I. 327

9 Conclusion

 328 We introduce FLEET, the ﬁrst benchmark and public leaderboard that provides a systematic, uniﬁed 329 measurement of few-shot NLP. It incorporates and introduces new best practices for few-shot evalua- 330 tion, including four transfer settings, textual labels for zero-shot evaluation, and novel analysis for 331 determining a sample size that optimizes statistical accuracy and precision while keeping computa- 332 tional burden low. Along with the benchmark, we present UniFew, a simple and strong baseline that 333 achieves results competitive with recent few-shot methods despite using trivial prompt engineering. 334 Finally, we release an extensible, open-source framework (used to train UniFew and generate FLEET) 335 that enables addition of NLP datasets and advanced sampling options to future benchmarks. 336 9

review.segment_text: Summary:
Fleet is a new benchmark and leaderboard that combines previous work on few-shot text classification.
While there are no new tasks, the new benhmark adds value by combining complimentary lines of work in a well designed evaluation framework.
Main Review:
This paper presents a new benchmark and associated leaderboard that aggregates text classification tasks from three previous works on few-shot learning.
The tasks are chosen to cover a range of domain, task, and learning transfer.
There is a detailed investigation of the trade-off between large test sets with few test episodes, and smaller test sets with many test episodes.
The test setting is chosen to maximise precision of the benchmark given a moderate compute budget.
The paper presents a new prompt-based approach to few-shot learning that converts each of the classification tasks into a multi-choice QA task.
The details of this conversion are not given in the paper and I would like to see them listed.
review.explanation: It is discussed in the paper, the authors overlooked it.

review.segment_text: Comparisons are also made to previous models that were applied to some subset of the tasks included in Fleet.

While this paper does not introduce any new tasks or evaluation methodologies, it does add value by combining several lines of complimentary work on few-shot learning into a single evaluation framework that has been well designed.
The prompt based UniFew baseline also seems both simple and effective, although I would like to see more details of the prompt template design in the main paper.
review.explanation: Details about Unifew, including the exact prompt templates used for each task are already included in the appendices C and D (this is mentioned in lines 280-281 in the paper). The author also have included source code to facilitate replication. The reviewer overlooked them.

review.segment_text: Limitations And Societal Impact:
The authors point out that Fleet is limited by it's restriction to text-classification tasks.
It is clearly not a defnitive benchmark, but still valuable.
The paper hints at the design of templates for the UniFew baseline but does not provide enough details for replication.

The benchmark only includes classification tasks and in English only.

The authors of this paper present a few-shot NLP benchmark called FLEET.
FLEET consists of a group of NLP datasets and evaluates four transfer settings: class transfer, domain transfer, task transfer, and pre-train transfer.

review.segment_text: Summary:
This paper proposes FLEET, a benchmark for few-shot learning in NLP.

FLEET is comprised of different few-shot settings (new tasks, label sets, or domains at test time), different amount of training examples ("shots"), and meta-learning strategies (w/ and w/o meta learning).
The paper goes through the design decisions behind FLEET and detail its construction.
Finally, they present a baseline based on UnifiedQA, wherein they reformulate downstream tasks as QA and then finetune the model on downstream tasks.
Main Review:
First, the benchmark contains a lot of different settings.
On one hand, this is a positive as it allows many different types of research to be conducted with the data.

On the other hand, it practically makes understanding, reporting, and using the benchmark a bit messy. For example, people will report very specific settings such as FLEET with {4-shot, with meta learning, task transfer}.
review.explanation: FLEET reports aggregates of 1-5 shot tests.

review.segment_text: More generally, there is often a tradeoff when constructing datasets of "do we focus on specific problems/settings we think are interesting" versus "do we build datasets that many people could use in different settings". This paper is a very extreme on trying to satisfy the second question: rather than trying to take a stand on what the community should work on, it tries to do a bit of everything.
review.explanation: A general comment on the topic selection of the paper, providing an opinion which is not substantiated.

review.segment_text: Second, a common criticism of GLUE and other benchmarks which applies to FLEET is that the benchmarks (1) simply repackage and resell other datasets as a new benchmark without adding substantial new value and (2) contain a relatively ad-hoc selection of individual datasets. FLEET is similar in that it sort of throws together a collection of tasks (sentiment, NLI, etc.) mainly guided by low-level reasons (e.g., the class imbalances) rather than higher-level ones (e.g., based on practical few-shot scenarios, different types of reasoning, tests of spurious correlations, etc. ).
review.topic_class_1: lack of novelty and design justification
review.explanation: These reviews minimize the paper contribution. Paper provides a detailed explanation of decisions for task selection.

review.segment_text: Third, a lower-level point is that I think few-shot benchmarks should contain multiple prompts / label descriptions for each dataset.
There can be high variance across different prompts (Zhao et al. ICML 2021, Gao et al. ACL 2021, etc.)
and so I think the reaction to this should be to report accuracy across multiple different prompts.
Finally, the proposed method is extremely similar to this concurrent work https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04670.
This is not a negative or a positive, I am simply pointing this out as an FYI to the authors, as they should probably cite/discuss this in a future version of their draft.
Limitations And Societal Impact:
Yes.

title: Ensembles and Cocktails: Robust Finetuning for Natural Language Generation
body_text:
E NSEMBLES AND C OCKTAILS : R OBUST F INETUNING FOR N ATURAL L ANGUAGE G ENERATION

 Anonymous authors Paper under double-blind review

A BSTRACT

 When ﬁnetuning a pretrained language model for natural language generation tasks, one is currently faced with a tradeoff. Lightweight ﬁnetuning (e.g., preﬁx- tuning, adapters), which freezes all or most of the parameters of the pretrained model, has been shown to achieve stronger out-of-distribution (OOD) performance than full ﬁnetuning , which tunes all of the parameters. However, lightweight ﬁnetuning can underperform full ﬁnetuning in-distribution (ID). In this work, we present methods to combine the beneﬁts of full and lightweight ﬁnetuning, achieving strong performance both ID and OOD. First, we show that an ensemble of the lightweight and full ﬁnetuning models achieves the best of both worlds: performance matching the better of full and lightweight ﬁnetuning, both ID and OOD. Second, we show that we can achieve similar improvements using a single model instead of two with our proposed cocktail ﬁnetuning , which augments full ﬁnetuning via distillation from a lightweight model. Finally, we provide some explanatory theory in a multiclass logistic regression setting with a large number of classes, describing how distillation on ID data can transfer the OOD behavior of one model to another.

1 I NTRODUCTION

 When ﬁnetuning a pretrained language model for natural language generation tasks like summariza- tion (Narayanan et al., 2018) and table-to-text (Gar- dent et al., 2017), one is currently faced with a tradeoff. One can achieve strong in-distribution (ID) performance or strong out-of-distribution (OOD) performance—but not both—by choosing one of two families of ﬁnetuning approaches. Finetuning all pa- rameters of the pretrained language model achieves strong ID performance (Howard & Ruder, 2018). We call this full ﬁnetuning . Alternatively, freezing most of the pretrained parameters during ﬁnetuning, in e.g., adapters (Rebufﬁ et al., 2017; Houlsby et al., 2019a), preﬁx-tuning (Li & Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021) and bitﬁt (Zaken et al., 2021), achieves stronger OOD performance than full ﬁnetuning (Li & Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021), but worse ID performance. We call these methods lightweight ﬁnetuning . In this work, we are the ﬁrst to demonstrate that this tradeoff is not necessary in natural language genera- tion: we can achieve the best of full and lightweight ﬁnetuning both ID and OOD. We test this across three natural language generation tasks in English: summarization (Narayanan et al., 2018), table-to-text (Gardent et al., 2017), and open-domain question answering (Roberts et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2019a), and two lightweight ﬁnetuning methods: adapters and preﬁx-tuning. Achieving the best of both worlds is important since on average across our datasets and lightweight ﬁnetuning methods, full 1 ﬁnetuning achieves only 84% of the OOD performance of lightweight ﬁnetuning, and lightweight ﬁnetuing achieves only 81% of the ID performance of full ﬁnetuning. We present two methods for achieving the best of full and lightweight ﬁnetuning. We ﬁrst show that a weighted ensemble of one full ﬁnetuning model and one lightweight ﬁnetuning model achieves performance comparable to the best of the two, both ID and OOD. To avoid running two models at once, we propose cocktail ﬁnetuning : ﬁrst train a lightweight ﬁnetuning model, and then train a full ﬁnetuning model on a mixture of student-teacher distillation loss (Bucil˘a et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) (with the lightweight model as teacher) and cross-entropy loss, on the original ID data. 1 The ensemble weight (resp. the cocktail mixture loss weight) is chosen to optimize for ID performance, and we observe that the resultant model achieves comparable OOD performance to lightweight ﬁnetuning. Our work contributes to an ongoing realization in machine learning: robust models that deviate minimally from a pretrained model can be gainfully combined with a model adapted more precisely to a speciﬁc dataset. Most saliently, in concurrent work, Wortsman et al. (2021) ﬁnd that zero- shot image recognition through CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) can be combined with a ﬁnetuned network to perform well ID and OOD. Our work demonstrates that similar results hold true in natural language generation as well. We draw from simple, well-known methods: ensembles, student-teacher distillation (Abnar et al., 2020; Hinton et al., 2015)—but our application to achieving the best of ID and OOD performance in natural language generation is novel. To better understand how cocktail ﬁnetuning can transfer the out-of-distribution behavior of the lightweight ﬁnetuning model when distilling only on in-distribution data , we theoretically study multiclass logistic regression with a large number of output classes, viewing language generation as a classiﬁcation problem over a large output space. We study a distribution shift setting where not all classes are seen in the ID training data (as is true in language generation due to Zipf’s law (Zipf, 1949)), and getting good OOD accuracy requires generalizing to unseen outputs. First, we prove that a model trained with gradient descent cannot distinguish the unseen output classes, leading to poor OOD accuracy. Second, we prove that distilling a teacher model with good OOD accuracy on only ID training data can transfer the OOD behavior of the teacher to the student, such that the student and teacher make the same prediction on any new input. As a result, the student also has good OOD accuracy. In summary, we present two simple methods—ensembling and cocktail ﬁnetuning—for achieving strong ID and OOD natural language generation with only the original ID data, achieving the “best of both worlds” of full and lightweight ﬁnetuning methods.

2 R ELATED W ORK

 Lightweight ﬁnetuning. Recently, as pretrained models scale up in the number of parameters, lightweight ﬁnetuning techniques have been developed to avoid updating all of the parameters. These techniques update a subset of the parameters (Zaken et al., 2021), introduce a small number of new parameters between layers of the model (called “adapters”) (Rebufﬁ et al., 2017; Houlsby et al., 2019b; Pfeiffer et al., 2020), or learn auxiliary inputs that are prepended to the models inputs (called “prompts”) (Shin et al., 2020; Li & Liang, 2021; Qin & Eisner, 2021; Liu et al., 2021b; Logan IV et al., 2021; and see Liu et al., 2021a for a survey). These techniques empirically have the beneﬁt of being able to achieve strong out-of-distribution extrapolation performance at the cost of worse in-distribution performance compared to full ﬁnetuning models both in classiﬁcation and generation settings (Li & Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021; Utama et al., 2021). In our work, we aim to overcome this trade-off by proposing techniques for achieving the best of both worlds, with a focus on language generation. Student-teacher distillation. Bucilu ˇ a et al. (2006) introduce distillation for compressing large ensembles into smaller, faster, more efﬁcient models, and Hinton et al. (2015) generalize their method and call it knowledge distillation. Kasai et al. (2021) distill Transformers into RNNs for linear-time inference. Abnar et al. (2020) show that knowledge distillation can transfer the inductive bias of one architecture to another: for example, distilling an LSTM to a Transformer leads to a Transformer with 1 We use the term cocktail as it is a refreshing mixture involving distillation. 2 representations that are more similar to independently trained LSTMs than independently trained Transformers. The efﬁciacy of our proposed cocktail ﬁnetuning is surprising even in context of these results, as it empirically transfers just the strong OOD performance of the teacher lightweight model to the student, while not transferring the weak ID performance. Robust ﬁnetuning in vision. In concurrent work, Wortsman et al. (2021) propose a similar ap- proach to ours, but focus on image classiﬁcation: they combine a full ﬁnetuning model with a lightweight ﬁnetuning (linear probe) model by ensembling the two models in weight space, and show that their approach maintains both good ID and OOD performance. It is yet surprising that in the structured prediction setting of natural language generation, we further show that we can achieve high OOD performance even when weight-space ensembling is impossible (for instance, since there are weights not held in common between the full ﬁnetuning model and an optimized prompt). Moreover, we further this line of work by providing a theoretical study into how distillation can transfer OOD behavior while only using ID data. Self-training for robustness. In adversarial robustness, standard models achieve good accuracy on clean examples but are not robust to adversarial examples, while adversarially trained models are more robust but are less accurate on clean examples. Raghunathan et al. (2020) show that the beneﬁts of these two models can be combined using robust self-training (RST) (Carmon et al., 2019; Uesato et al., 2019; Najaﬁ et al., 2019) on unlabeled data to improve clean and robust accuracy. Similarly, Khani & Liang (2021) show that RST can be used to combine models with spurious features removed (which are more robust) and without removing spurious features (which are more accurate). In general OOD robustness, In-N-Out (Xie et al., 2021) uses self-training to transfer the robustness beneﬁts of a model pre-trained with auxiliary self-supervision to a model trained with extra auxiliary features. Berthelot et al. (2021) use unlabeled data and a consistency regularization loss for domain adaptation. While many of these methods combine the beneﬁts of two models or use a self-training/distillation loss to improve robustness, cocktail ﬁnetuning differs in that it performs distillation only on ID training data without any additional ID or OOD unlabeled examples.

3 P ROBLEM S TATEMENT 3.1 S ETUP

 We consider a conditional generation task from an input space X (e.g., a news article) to an output space Y (e.g., a summary of the article), where both spaces consist of sequences of tokens from a shared vocabulary V . Data. Let P id and P ood denote the distribution of ( x, y ) pairs in-distribution and out-of-distribution, respectively, where x ∈ X and y ∈ Y . In summarization, P id may consist of articles about world and business news while P ood consists of health and technology news. The training data D train and validation data D val consist of n and n val in-distribution ( x, y ) pairs respectively, drawn from P id . Model and metrics. Let q γ ( y | x ) = (cid:81) len ( y ) j =1 q γ ( y j | x, y <j ) be a pretrained neural autoregressive sequence model with parameters γ . Finetuning (full or lightweight) produces a ﬁnetuned model p θ ( y | x ) from q γ , where θ denotes the set of trainable parameters. In full ﬁnetuning, θ is the same set of parameters as γ ; in lightweight ﬁnetuning, θ often refers to the parameters of inserted modules (e.g., adapters modules or preﬁxes). The ﬁnal predictor is f θ ( x ) which approximates arg max y p θ ( y | x ) through, e.g., beam search. The goal is to learn parameters θ such that the predictor f θ obtains good ID and OOD performance: where score may be deﬁned differently for each task (e.g., exact match score or BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002b)). 3

3.2 B ASELINE FINE - TUNING METHODS

 Full ﬁnetuning has been the defacto approach to adapt pretrained language models for downstream generation tasks (Lewis et al., 2020; Kale & Rastogi, 2020). Under this framework, the model p θ is initialized with its pretrained parameters γ , and we optimize the following log-likelihood objective. where the set of trainable parameters θ refer to the set of pretrained parameters γ . Lightweight ﬁnetuning is another family of adaptation approaches, which freezes most of the pretrained parameters and augments the model with small trainable modules. Lightweight ﬁnetuning shares the same training objective as full ﬁnetuning, but the trainable parameters θ are different. Within the lightweight ﬁnetuning family, we focus on adapter-tuning (Houlsby et al., 2019a) and preﬁx-tuning (Li & Liang, 2021). Both approaches keep the pretrained parameters intact. Adapter- tuning inserts task-speciﬁc MLP layers between each layer of the pretrained language models, and the trainable parameter θ consists of these inserted MLP parameters. Preﬁx-tuning prepends a sequence of trainable, task-speciﬁc preﬁx vectors to the input, and θ consists of these preﬁx parameters. 2

4 E XPERIMENT S ETUP 4.1 D ATASETS AND M ETRICS

 Summarization. We use the XSUM (Narayan et al., 2018) dataset, which is an abstractive sum- marization dataset on BBC news articles. Each example is labeled with a news category. We select world, UK and business categories to be in-distribution and let the remaining news categories such as health and technology to be out-of-distribution. We report the ROUGE-2 scores (Lin, 2004). Open-domain, closed-book QA (Open-QA). We use the open-domain variant (Lee et al., 2019b) of the Natural Questions dataset (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) as the in-distribution data and the Web Questions dataset (Berant et al., 2013) as the out-of-distribution data. The distribution shift is induced by different data collection process and their year of collection (roughly 2018 versus 2013). We 2 For speciﬁcs of these methods, see their respective papers . 4 report the exact match accuracy. Note that this task, unlike most QA (e.g., SQuAD (Rajpurkar et al., 2016)), does not provide systems with a text from which to extract answers. Roberts et al. (2020) demonstrated that one could ﬁnetune an LM to generate answers from knowledge stored during pretraining.

4.2 M ODEL A RCHITECTURES AND H YPERPARAMETERS

 We use GPT-2-medium (Radford et al., 2019) as the pretrained model for table-to-text and open- domain QA tasks. GPT-2 is an autoregressive language model; therefore, we parametrize p θ ( y | x ) by concatenating x , a separator token, and y (e.g., [x; SEP; y]). We deﬁne the loss function to sum over the token losses that correspond to y . We use BART-large (Lewis et al., 2020) as the pretrained model for the summarization task. BART uses an encoder-decoder architecture and parametrizes p θ ( y | x ) by ﬁrst feeding x to the encoder, and decoding y conditioned on the encoder representation. For open-domain closed-book QA, this is to our knowledge the ﬁrst time GPT-2 has been ﬁnetuned for the task. We used separate development OOD data to test a handful ( < 10) of hyperparameter settings to determine whether we’d observe a similar ID/OOD tradeoff to the other tasks. We note this because, in general, one cannot do hyperparameter optimization on OOD data; we did this to provide another testbed for our methods. Our implementation is based on the Hugging Face Transformers package (Wolf et al., 2020). We use most of the hyperparameters suggested by the Hugging Face default setup. The hyperparameters we tune include the number of epochs, batch size, learning rate, and preﬁx length (for preﬁx-tuning), all reported in Table 3 in the appendix.

5 R ESULTS OF FULL AND LIGHTWEIGHT FINETUNING

 There is a trade-off in ID/OOD performance when choosing between full ﬁnetuning and lightweight ﬁnetuning: full ﬁnetuning consistently outperform in-distribution, whereas lightweight ﬁnetuning consistently outperform out-of-distribution (Li & Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021). To quantify this trade-off, we examine the generation performance of both methods on ID and OOD data. As shown in Table 2, when evaluating in-distribution, full ﬁnetuning achieves the stronger results (denoting this ID skyline as 100%), whereas lightweight ﬁnetuning achieves only 81% of the skyline, on average. When evaluating out-of-distribution, lightweight ﬁnetuning achieves stronger result (denoting this OOD skyline as 100%), whereas full ﬁnetuning achieves only 84% of the skyline. Lightweight ﬁnetuning tends to produce models that are more robust at the cost of good ID performance; Full ﬁnetuning produces models that attain good ID performance at the cost of OOD performance. 3

 As we observe in Section 5, full ﬁnetuning models attain better ID performance but worse OOD performance, whereas lightweight ﬁnetuning models attain better OOD performance at the cost of good ID performance. Is it possible to achieve both good ID and OOD performance simultaneously? In this section, we show that a simple ensemble of the two methods accomplishes this. First, we train a lightweight ﬁnetuning model p ( (cid:96) ) and a full ﬁnetuning model p ( f) on D train . At decoding time, we combine the prediction of the p ( (cid:96) ) and p ( f) by interpolating them at each token. At each time step t , both models output a next token distribution conditioned on the common history y <t , and the two distributions are interpolated with a mixture weight λ . The output is generated by beam searching the ensemble distribution p (Ens) ( y t | x, y <t ) . 3 Though it is worth noting again that for open-domain QA, we performed a small amount of manual, exploratory hyperparameter optimization to optimize the ID of full ﬁnetuning and the OOD of lightweight ﬁnetuning. 5 three , and ensembles with mixture coefﬁcients in each chosen by in-distribution validation performance. 6.1 C HOOSING THE M IXTURE W EIGHT λ

 We start with a set of { λ i } K i =1 where λ i ∈ [0 , 1] . For example we use λ ∈ { 0 ., 0 . 1 , 0 . 25 , 0 . 5 , 0 . 75 , 0 . 9 , 1 . 0 } in this experiment. We choose the mixture weight λ i that attains the best score on D val . This method of choosing λ is useful because (1) it crucially does not use OOD data, which is typically unaccessible at model selection time, and (2) it guarantees that ID performance is not sacriﬁced, because we can match ID performance by setting λ = 0 .

6.2 R ESULTS

 As shown in Table 2, the ensemble matches and slightly outperforms both the ID performance skyline (achieved by full ﬁnetuning) and the OOD performance skyline (achieved by lightweight ﬁnetuning). Comparing with the weaker candidates ID and OOD, and averaging across 6 settings (3 datasets, two lightweight ﬁnetuning methods,) the ensemble achieves a 37% improvement over the weaker ID candidate (i.e, lightweight ﬁnetuning) and a 24% relative improvement over the weaker OOD candidate (i.e., full ﬁnetuning). Therefore, the ensemble—unlike lightweight and full ﬁnetuning— achieves the best of both worlds: performance matching the better of full and lightweight ﬁnetuning, for both ID and OOD.

6.3 R UNTIME AND M EMORY

 Despite its ability to combine the best of both worlds, ensembling is expensive at inference time because two models are run simultaneously, doubling the amount of GPU memory required. Fur- thermore, two forward passes are required, doubling the runtime for decoding. 4 For deployment efﬁciency, it’s better to have a single model at inference time.

10 C ONCLUSION

 Considered together, our work and the work of Wortsman et al. (2021) provide strong cross-modal evidence that simple ensembles of models that have minimally deviated from pretraining (for them, zero-shot; for us, lightweight ﬁnetuning models) with full ﬁnetuning models provides strong ID and OOD accuracy. The reasons for this “best of both worlds” behavior are still poorly understood, motivating future work. Since ensemble models effectively weight by model conﬁdence (though modulated by λ ), one explanation may be that lightweight ﬁnetuning models are less conﬁdent than full ﬁnetuning models in-distribution, yet more conﬁdent out-of-distribution. In summary, we provide simple, effective methods for achieving the best of lightweight and full ﬁnetuning—strong OOD and ID performance—in language generation. Our cocktail ﬁnetuning provides system builders with the opportunity to optimize for in-distribution performance (in choosing lambda), often beating full ﬁnetuning, while resting assured that the out-of-distribution performance (i.e., what they observe with real users) will likely be higher than had they performed full ﬁnetuning. 9

E THICS STATEMENT

 The methods presented in this work have the potential to improve a wide range of natural language generation tasks. Natural language generation has known dual-use issues, like scaling misinformation generation and generating naturalistic text in scams. The WebNLG XSUM, Natural Questions and WebQuestions datasets we evaluate on contain personal information (though public and published) information about real people and organizations.

review.segment_text: Summary Of The Paper:
This paper proposes an ensemble model between a full fine-tuning model and a parameter-efficient fine-tuning model to improve the out-of-distribution (OOD) performance of a full fine-tuning model.

The proposed method is inspired by the observation that full fine-tuning model achieves good in-distribution (ID) performance while parameter-efficient finetuning model achieves better OOD performance.

There are two ensembling methods presented in the paper: linear interpolation between the predictions of the two models; and distill from the predictions of a parameter-efficient model with ID training data.
Improved OOD performance is observed with this ensemble method.
Main Review:
Strengths:
The writing is generally clear.
The paper is addressing an important phenomenon that parameter-efficient tuning which has deficient ID performance, while full fine-tuning has worse OOD performance.
Weakness:
First of all, the presented methodology is not well motivated.
Parameter-efficient tuning aims to reduce number of parameters that need to save for each task by only fine-tuning a small number of additional parameters.
However, the proposed method produces an ensemble model that fine-tunes all parameters, losing the parameter-efficiency.

If the goal of this paper is to improve the OOD performance of full fine-tuning, it should compare with methods that improve OOD performance which has a vast amount of related work. And this literature review is also missing from the paper. On the other hand, if the goal of this paper is to improve the ID performance of parameter-efficient tuning, then it should propose a method for improving parameter-efficient tuning methods rather than combine it with full fine-tuning.

Summary Of The Paper:

The present paper first discusses the trade-off between performance for out-of-domain data and in-domain data with respect to whether the model is fully fine-tuned or lightweight fine-tuned on NLG tasks.
Second, it argues that such a trade-off is not necessary if one can make use of both of these two fine-tuning schema in a clever way.

To this end, it proposes cocktail fine-tuning, which augments full fine-tuning via distillation from a lightweight model and which achieves equal performance as an ensemble of the two fine-tuning schema.
At length, this paper also explains the behavior of the cocktail fine-tuning through a toy model.
Main Review:
The current paper looks perfect up to section 4.
It properly discusses different fine-tuning schema as well as the trade-off between OOD performance and ID performance with respect to the use of a fune-tuning scheme.
It properly defines the problem (i.e., the trade-off) and proposes a simple yet effective way to overcome it.
It tests its method on three different NLG tasks: Table2Text Generation, Summarisation, and QA.
However, starting from section 5, it makes me hard to recommend an acceptance for this paper in the current format.
This is because of two major concerns.
One is that the interpretations of experimental results are problematic, weight might make the rest discussions and conclusions do not stand anymore.
In section 5, regarding Table 2, the authors say "when evaluating ID, full fine-tuning achieves the stronger results, whereas lightweight fine-tuning achieves only 81% of the skyline on average".
This statement is only true "on average" and overlooks the huge differences between different tasks.
For example, for ID data of the Data2Text task, full fine-tuning achieves a score of 63.25 while lightweight fine-tuning achieve 63.18.
There is no significant difference between the performance on ID of these two schema.
Meanwhile, in a similar vein, for OOD samples of the summarisation task, I also found no significant difference between the two schema.
The situation described by the author only exists when doing question answering.

This suggests that such a trade-off is task-dependent to a large extent and it seems to me that if a task relies on the inputs in a more directed way (e.g., QA is often accomplished by simply copying text from inputs), then the trade-off is more significant and the proposed model is more useful.
